projectPolicy.note: Decisions for this practice app where the guide is silent or only says 'good practice'. Rules changed by this policy carry "policy": true.
projectPolicy.assignmentAlias: Accept <- as typed input for ←; always display it as ←.
projectPolicy.declarations: Variables that are not declared are an ERROR. This includes FOR loop variables, even though the guide's examples never declare them.
projectPolicy.keywordCase: Keywords not written in upper case are an ERROR.
projectPolicy.precedence: Only * / binding tighter than + - may be relied on. Any other mix of operator groups without parentheses is an ERROR.
projectPolicy.negativeNumbers: INT, DIV and MOD truncate toward zero.
projectPolicy.functionSet: The guide's functions plus the 2025 exam-insert functions.
projectPolicy.indentation: One tab per indent level, the same as the O Level file.

ruleLevels.required: The guide says must / must never / is written as – a hard syntax rule.
ruleLevels.goodPractice: The guide calls it good practice / advisable – a style rule, not a syntax error.

meta.notation: Text in <angle brackets> is a meta-variable (placeholder), as in Backus-Naur Form. '...' means 'more of the same'.

font.rule: Monospaced (fixed-width) font such as Courier New, consistent size throughout.

indentation.rule: Lines contained within a statement on a previous line are indented by one tab per level. The guide uses 3 spaces.
The guide says THEN and ELSE may be indented by only 2 spaces. In this file, ELSE lines up with its IF and statements are one tab in.
Indentation may be omitted when line numbers are used.
Statements should fit on one line where possible; continuation lines are aligned for readability.

case.rule: Keywords are UPPER-CASE, e.g. IF, REPEAT, PROCEDURE. Lower-case keywords (if, endif) are an error.
Identifiers are mixed case (PascalCase), capital letter at the start of each word, e.g. NumberOfPlayers.

lineNumbering.rule: Line numbers appear to the left, clearly separated from the code.
Line numbers are consecutive; gaps mean code is missing and this will be stated.
Each statement is numbered; continuation lines of a statement are not numbered.

comments.rule: Comments start with // and run to the end of the line.
Multi-line comments: every line starts with //. There is no block-comment syntax.
A comment normally goes on its own line before the code it refers to, at the same indentation.
A short comment about a single line may go at the end of that line.

formatting.example:
// this procedure swaps
// values of X and Y
PROCEDURE SWAP(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER)
	Temp ← X // temporarily store X
	X ← Y
	Y ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE

dataTypes.name: REAL
dataTypes.description: A number that can have a fractional part
dataTypes.literal: Always at least one digit on BOTH sides of the decimal point, adding zeros if needed

dataTypes.name: STRING
dataTypes.description: A sequence of zero or more characters
dataTypes.literal: Between double quotes; may be empty

dataTypes.name: BOOLEAN
dataTypes.description: The logical values TRUE and FALSE

dataTypes.name: DATE
dataTypes.literal: Normally dd/mm/yyyy; good practice to state that the value is a DATE and explain the format

rules.rule: Only letters A–Z / a–z, digits 0–9 and underscore _.
Must start with a letter, not a digit.
No accented letters.
Keywords must never be used as identifiers.
Identifiers are case-insensitive: Countdown and CountDown are the same name and must not be used as separate variables.
Use descriptive names.
Conventional single letters are allowed, e.g. i, j for array indices, X, Y for coordinates.
Use mixed case (PascalCase).
Every variable must be declared with DECLARE before use, including FOR loop variables. The guide only calls this good practice; this app makes it an error.
A variable that is declared but never assigned holds a random value of its declared type. Reading it is not an error, but the result is unpredictable.
Variables declared inside a procedure, function or method are local to it. Parameters are local too.
The value must be a literal. A variable, another constant or an expression must never be used.
Constants use = (not ←) and have no data type annotation.
Use constants where they make code more readable or easier to update.
Declare constants at the start of the code, unless you want to limit their scope.
The left side must be a variable, which can be an array element or a field of a user-defined type.
The right side may be any expression that evaluates to the same data type as the variable.

arrays.description: Fixed-length structures of elements of the same data type, accessed by consecutive integer indices. The syllabus requires 1D and 2D arrays.

rules.rule: Square brackets [ ] enclose array indices.
Always state the lower bound explicitly; it defaults to 0 or 1 depending on the system.
A lower bound of 1 is generally used.
An index may be a literal or any expression that evaluates to a valid integer.
2D elements are accessed as Name[row, column] (one pair of brackets, comma-separated).
A whole array can be assigned to another of the same size and data type, e.g. SavedGame ← NoughtsAndCrosses.
Do not refer to a group of elements in one statement (e.g. StudentNames[1 TO 30] ← ""). Use a loop to assign them one at a time.

examples:
FOR Index ← 1 TO 30
	StudentNames[Index] ← ""
NEXT Index

rules.rule: Values are ordered as listed. + n and - n move forward or back through the list: Spring + 1 = Summer.
Values do not wrap. Going past either end is an error: Winter + 1 and Spring - 1 are errors.
In a TYPE definition, ^ before a data type means 'pointer to that type'.
Declaring a variable of a pointer type does not use ^, e.g. DECLARE MyPointer : TIntPointer.
^Variable (caret before) gives the address of that variable.
Pointer^ (caret after) dereferences: it reads the value stored at the address.

record.syntax:
TYPE <identifier1>
	DECLARE <identifier2> : <data type>
	DECLARE <identifier3> : <data type>
	...
ENDTYPE
examples:
TYPE StudentRecord
	DECLARE LastName : STRING
	DECLARE FirstName : STRING
	DECLARE DateOfBirth : DATE
	DECLARE YearGroup : INTEGER
	DECLARE FormGroup : CHAR
ENDTYPE

set.syntax:
TYPE <identifier1> = SET OF <data type>
DEFINE <identifier2> (value1, value2, value3, ...) : <identifier1>
examples:
TYPE LetterSet = SET OF CHAR
DEFINE Vowels ('A','E','I','O','U') : LetterSet

usageRules.rule: Once defined, a user-defined type can be used in declarations like any built-in type, including as an array element type.
Variables of the same user-defined type can be assigned to each other, e.g. Pupil2 ← Pupil1.
Fields are accessed with dot notation, e.g. Pupil1.LastName, Form[Index].YearGroup.

arithmetic.note: The result is REAL even when both operands are INTEGER.

arithmetic.negatives: Remainder has the sign of the dividend: -7 MOD 2 → -1

typeErrors.rule: Using an operator with a value of the wrong type is an error.

rules.rule: = compares two items of the same type.
REAL and INTEGER can be compared with each other.
CHAR and STRING can be compared with each other.
Comparing CHAR or STRING values is case-sensitive: "Program" = "program" is FALSE.
Two records cannot be compared.

Two strings, or two chars, are equal only if they have the same length and the same characters in the same positions (case-sensitive). "a" = "a" and 'a' = 'a' are TRUE; "a" = "A" and "a" = "a " are FALSE.

logical.note: These are the only logic operators.

string.note: Can also join a CHAR with a STRING (insert-2025-21).

precedence.statedByGuide: * and / bind tighter than + and - (normal maths convention).

rules.rule: Use parentheses to make the order of operations explicit in complex arithmetic, relational and logical expressions.
Without parentheses, the only precedence you may rely on is * / over + -. Mixing any other operator groups without parentheses is an error.
rules.comment: Stricter than the guide on purpose: brackets are never wrong in an exam, but relying on an unstated order can cost marks. This teaches students the safe habit.
allowedWithoutParentheses: any mix of multiplicative and additive (* / over + -)
a chain of one operator group (left to right), e.g. A + B - C, A & B & C, A AND B AND C

builtInFunctions.note: Functions without a "source" field come from the guide. Functions tagged "source": "insert-2025-21" come from the May/June 2025 exam insert. The insert does not list LCASE or UCASE; it uses TO_LOWER and TO_UPPER instead.

rules.rule: Each function returns an error if the call is not properly formed.
Passing parameters of the wrong type or with an invalid value is also an error.
A string of length 1 can be treated as either CHAR or STRING.
A CHAR can be assigned to, or concatenated with, a STRING.
A STRING longer than 1 character cannot be assigned to a CHAR.
String functions are always provided in the exam; the ones below are a basic set.

In Paper 2 the insert is the authority on function names. It has no LCASE or UCASE; use TO_LOWER and TO_UPPER, which take a CHAR or a STRING. LCASE and UCASE (guide, CHAR only) are kept for completeness.
Explain any language-specific string operations (searching, splitting) or number-to-string formatting, since they vary between systems.

string.name: RIGHT
string.signature: RIGHT(ThisString : STRING, x : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING
string.description: Returns the rightmost x characters of ThisString

string.name: MID
string.signature: MID(ThisString : STRING, x : INTEGER, y : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING
string.description: Returns a string of length y starting at position x (positions start at 1)

string.name: LCASE
string.description: Returns the lower-case version of ThisChar; anything that is not an upper-case letter is returned unchanged

string.name: UCASE
string.description: Returns the upper-case version of ThisChar; anything that is not a lower-case letter is returned unchanged

string.name: LEFT
string.signature: LEFT(ThisString : STRING, x : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING
string.description: Returns the leftmost x characters of ThisString

string.name: TO_UPPER
string.description: Returns x with every character converted to upper case, keeping the same type

string.name: TO_LOWER
string.description: Returns x with every character converted to lower case, keeping the same type

string.name: NUM_TO_STR
string.description: Returns the string form of a number; a negative number gives a string starting with '-'

string.name: STR_TO_NUM
string.description: Returns the number a string represents; a string starting with '-' gives a negative value

string.name: IS_NUM
string.description: Returns TRUE if ThisString is a valid number

string.name: ASC
string.description: Returns the ASCII value of ThisChar

string.name: CHR
string.description: Returns the character with ASCII value x

numeric.name: INT
numeric.description: Returns the integer part of x, truncating toward zero (policy for negatives)

numeric.name: RAND
numeric.description: Returns a random REAL from 0 up to but not including x

date.name: DAYINDEX
date.description: Returns the day of the week, where Sunday = 1, Monday = 2, and so on

date.name: SETDATE
date.signature: SETDATE(Day, Month, Year : INTEGER) RETURNS DATE

dateFormat.rule: Dates are DD/MM/YYYY unless stated otherwise.

file.name: EOF
file.description: TRUE if there are no more lines to read (or an empty file is open for READ), otherwise FALSE. The insert adds that calling EOF on a file not open in READ mode is an error.

rules.rule: The target must be a variable, which can be an array element or a field of a user-defined type.
Several values separated by commas can be output in one statement.
Each OUTPUT statement prints on a new line. All values in one OUTPUT (joined with commas or &) stay on that line, with no extra spaces added.
ELSE is optional.
Every IF ends with ENDIF, including nested IFs.
There is no ELSEIF keyword in the guide; use a nested IF inside ELSE, or a CASE statement.

if.example:
IF ChallengerScore > ChampionScore THEN
	IF ChallengerScore > HighestScore THEN
		OUTPUT ChallengerName, " is champion and highest scorer"
	ELSE
		OUTPUT ChallengerName, " is the new champion"
	ENDIF
ELSE
	OUTPUT ChampionName, " is still the champion"
	IF ChampionScore > HighestScore THEN
		OUTPUT ChampionName, " is also the highest scorer"
	ENDIF
ENDIF

rules.rule: The subject is a variable identifier: CASE OF <identifier>.
Each branch is written <value> : <statement(s)>; extra statements go on following lines, one tab further in than the clause.
A branch value can be a range: <value1> TO <value2>.
OTHERWISE is optional; if present, it must be the last case.
Cases are tested in order. The first match runs, then control goes to the line after ENDCASE; later cases are not tested (no fall-through).
OTHERWISE runs only if no earlier case matched.

case.example:
INPUT Move
CASE OF Move
	'W' : Position ← Position - 10
	'S' : Position ← Position + 10
	'A' : Position ← Position - 1
	'D' : Position ← Position + 1
	OTHERWISE : CALL Beep
ENDCASE

rules.rule: The loop variable must be an INTEGER variable, and (policy) it must be declared.
value1, value2 and the STEP increment must be expressions that evaluate to integers.
Bounds are inclusive: the variable takes every value from value1 to value2.
If value1 = value2 the body runs once; if value1 > value2 (with no STEP) it runs zero times.
With STEP, the variable starts at value1 and changes by increment each time; the loop stops once it goes past value2.
STEP can be negative, e.g. FOR Position ← 20 TO 10 STEP -1.
Repeat the loop variable after NEXT, especially in nested loops.

for.example:
Total ← 0
FOR Row ← 1 TO MaxRow
	RowTotal ← 0
	FOR Column ← 1 TO 10
		RowTotal ← RowTotal + Amount[Row, Column]
	NEXT Column
	OUTPUT "Total for Row ", Row, " is ", RowTotal
	Total ← Total + RowTotal
NEXT Row
OUTPUT "The grand total is ", Total

rules.rule: The condition must evaluate to BOOLEAN.
The body always runs at least once.
The condition is tested after the body; the loop stops when it is TRUE.

repeat.example:
REPEAT
	OUTPUT "Please enter the password"
	INPUT Password
UNTIL Password = "Secret"

rules.rule: The condition must evaluate to BOOLEAN.
There is no DO keyword after the condition.
The condition is tested before each pass; the loop stops when it is FALSE.
If the condition is FALSE on the first test, the body never runs.

general.rule: Define before use. Code inside a subroutine may call subroutines defined anywhere in the file, including ones further down. A statement outside any subroutine may only call subroutine X if X, and every subroutine X calls directly or indirectly, is defined above that statement. Otherwise it is an error. The guide has no rule about placement; its 8.1 example follows this rule.
general.validExample:
PROCEDURE A()
	CALL B()
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE B()
	OUTPUT "Hi"
ENDPROCEDURE

CALL A()
general.invalidExample:
PROCEDURE A()
	CALL B()
ENDPROCEDURE

CALL A()   // error: B is not defined yet

PROCEDURE B()
	OUTPUT "Hi"
ENDPROCEDURE

general.rule: Using RETURN inside a procedure is an error.

rules.rule: Procedures are called with the CALL keyword; a call is a complete statement.
Arguments must have the correct data types and be in the same order as the parameters in the definition.
Parameters act as variables inside the procedure body.
Empty parentheses () are written even when there are no parameters, in both the definition and the call.

procedure.example:
PROCEDURE DefaultSquare()
	CALL Square(100)
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE Square(Size : INTEGER)
	FOR Side ← 1 TO 4
		CALL MoveForward(Size)
		CALL Turn(90)
	NEXT Side
ENDPROCEDURE

IF Size = Default THEN
	CALL DefaultSquare()
ELSE
	CALL Square(Size)
ENDIF

syntax.withParams:
FUNCTION <identifier>(<param1> : <data type>, <param2> : <data type>, ...) RETURNS <data type>
	<statement(s)>
ENDFUNCTION

rules.rule: The header states the return type with RETURNS <data type>. Note RETURNS in the header and RETURN in the body.
A function returns exactly one value.
RETURN is normally the last statement, but runs immediately wherever it appears; any code after it is skipped.
Never use CALL with a function. A function call is not a complete statement; it is only used inside an expression.
The returned value replaces the call in the expression, which is then evaluated.
Do not pass parameters to a function by reference (no BYREF in functions).
Any function used in an exam will be defined in the question.

function.example:
FUNCTION Max(Number1 : INTEGER, Number2 : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
	IF Number1 > Number2 THEN
		RETURN Number1
	ELSE
		RETURN Number2
	ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT "Penalty Fine = ", Max(10, Distance*2)

rules.rule: BYVAL or BYREF goes before the parameter in the definition, not in the call.
If several parameters use the same method, the keyword need not be repeated. In SWAP(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER), both X and Y are BYREF.
BYVAL is the default: if no method is given, parameters are passed BYVAL.

parameterPassing.example:
PROCEDURE SWAP(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER)
	Temp ← X
	X ← Y
	Y ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE

text.description: Text files are lines of text, read or written one after another as strings.

modes.meaning: Write data to the file. Creates a new file; any existing data is lost.
Add data after any existing data

rules.rule: A file must be opened in a mode before any other file operation.
The file identifier is a string literal of the file name, or a STRING variable holding it.
A file is open in only one mode at a time.
READFILE needs READ mode and reads the next line into a STRING variable.
WRITEFILE needs WRITE or APPEND mode.
Close files with CLOSEFILE when they are no longer needed.
The usual read loop is WHILE NOT EOF(<file>).

text.example:
DECLARE LineOfText : STRING
OPENFILE "FileA.txt" FOR READ
OPENFILE "FileB.txt" FOR WRITE
WHILE NOT EOF("FileA.txt")
	READFILE "FileA.txt", LineOfText
	IF LineOfText = "" THEN
		WRITEFILE "FileB.txt", "-------------------------"
	ELSE
		WRITEFILE "FileB.txt", LineOfText
	ENDIF
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "FileA.txt"
CLOSEFILE "FileB.txt"

random.description: Random files hold fixed-length records. A file pointer can be moved to any record, which can then be read or written.

rules.rule: Random files are opened with mode RANDOM.
The SEEK address must evaluate to an integer, usually the number of records from the start of the file.
Explain how addresses are calculated.
GETRECORD reads the record at the file pointer into a variable of the matching type (usually a user-defined type).
PUTRECORD writes the variable at the file pointer, replacing any data already there.

random.example:
OPENFILE "StudentFile.Dat" FOR RANDOM
FOR Position ← 20 TO 10 STEP -1
	SEEK "StudentFile.Dat", Position
	GETRECORD "StudentFile.Dat", Pupil
	SEEK "StudentFile.Dat", Position + 1
	PUTRECORD "StudentFile.Dat", Pupil
NEXT Position
SEEK "StudentFile.Dat", 10
PUTRECORD "StudentFile.Dat", NewPupil
CLOSEFILE "StudentFile.Dat"

class.syntax:
CLASS <class name>
	<PUBLIC|PRIVATE> <attribute> : <data type>
	<PUBLIC|PRIVATE> PROCEDURE NEW(<params>)
		<statement(s)>
	ENDPROCEDURE
	...
ENDCLASS
class.inheritanceSyntax:
CLASS <class name> INHERITS <parent class name>
	...
ENDCLASS

rules.rule: Methods and properties are PUBLIC unless stated otherwise.
When access matters, PUBLIC or PRIVATE is written explicitly before the attribute or method.
Attributes are written <PUBLIC|PRIVATE> <name> : <type>, with no DECLARE keyword.
The constructor is a procedure named NEW.
Inheritance uses INHERITS; parent-class methods are called with SUPER, e.g. SUPER.NEW(GivenName).
Objects are created with <object> ← NEW <ClassName>(<args>).
Methods are called with dot notation, e.g. Player.GetAttempts().

CALL follows the same rule as ordinary subroutines. Procedure methods (including SUPER.NEW) need CALL; function methods never use CALL and only appear inside an expression. The guide's own examples leave CALL out for procedure methods, so those examples would be errors under this rule.

examples:
CLASS Pet
	PRIVATE Name : STRING
	PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenName : STRING)
		Name ← GivenName
	ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

CLASS Cat INHERITS Pet
	PRIVATE Breed : STRING
	PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenName : STRING, GivenBreed : STRING)
		CALL SUPER.NEW(GivenName)
		Breed ← GivenBreed
	ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

sourceErrata.issue: TIntPointer is declared as ^INTEGER but is then given the address of ThisSeason, which is a Season.
The record field is declared as FirstName but assigned as Pupil1.Firstname. This is valid because identifiers are case-insensitive, but inconsistent.
MOD is described as 'MOD or Modulus'. Only MOD is a keyword.
Logic operators are described as 'also called relational operators'. That is wrong: relational operators are the comparisons in 5.3.
The SWAP example uses Temp without declaring it, and the identifier SWAP is all upper case instead of mixed case.
MoveForward and Turn are never defined; treat them as given library procedures.
The example uses type Student, 'defined in Section 4.1', but 4.1 defines StudentRecord.
The file is opened as "StudentFile.Dat" but closed as "StudentFile.dat".
Player.SetAttempts(5) and SUPER.NEW(GivenName) call procedure methods without CALL. Under rule OOP-8 this file writes them as CALL Player.SetAttempts(5) and CALL SUPER.NEW(GivenName).
Cat declares PRIVATE Breed: INTEGER but assigns it GivenBreed : STRING. This file corrects Breed to STRING in its example.

ambiguities.issue: The guide only says * and / bind tighter than + and -. It does not place DIV, MOD, &, the relational operators, or NOT / AND / OR.
ambiguities.resolution: Require parentheses for any other mix of operator groups (see OP-2).

ambiguities.issue: The guide only lists 8 functions; exam inserts add more.
ambiguities.resolution: Added the functions from the 9618/21 May/June 2025 insert, tagged with source insert-2025-21.

ambiguities.topic: DIV / MOD / INT with negative numbers
ambiguities.issue: The guide does not say whether these truncate or floor.
ambiguities.resolution: All truncate toward zero: INT(-2.5) = -2, -7 DIV 2 = -3, -7 MOD 2 = -1.

ambiguities.issue: The example NextSeason ← MyPointer^ + 1 suggests that adding 1 to an enumerated value gives the next value. The guide does not say what happens after the last value (Winter + 1).
ambiguities.resolution: No wrapping; going past either end is an error (ENUM-2).

ambiguities.issue: Procedures need CALL, but the OOP examples leave CALL out for procedure methods.
ambiguities.resolution: Procedure methods need CALL; function methods never use it (OOP-8).

ambiguities.issue: Declaring variables is only 'good practice' in the guide.
ambiguities.resolution: A missing DECLARE is an error, including for FOR loop variables (see DEC-1).
<- is accepted as input and displayed as ←.

ambiguities.issue: The guide does not say whether string comparison is case-sensitive.
ambiguities.resolution: The 2025 insert says comparison is case-sensitive, and CHAR and STRING can be compared (REL-3, REL-4).

ambiguities.topic: OUTPUT, uninitialised variables, scope, string equality
ambiguities.resolution: Each OUTPUT goes on a new line (IO-3). Unassigned variables hold random values (DEC-2). Subroutine variables are local (DEC-3). String and char equality is an exact, case-sensitive match (REL-6).

ambiguities.issue: No source says how strings are ordered, e.g. whether "apple" < "banana" or "Z" < "a".
ambiguities.assumedDefault: Compare character by character using ASCII codes; a shorter string that is a prefix of a longer one comes first. So "Z" < "a" is TRUE.

ambiguities.issue: The guide does not say whether lower-case keywords are invalid.
ambiguities.resolution: They are an error, the same strictness as missing declarations (FMT-CASE-1).
